title: Bond Selloff Sends 30-Year Yield to 19-Year High as Fed Credibility Wavers
excerpt: Three FOMC dissenters wanted a rate hike, and the bond market's verdict on Chairman Warsh's inflation stance was swift and brutal.
body:
• The 30-year U.S. Treasury yield surged above 5.2%, its highest level since 2007, after the Fed held rates steady on Wednesday.
  • Three FOMC members dissented in favor of a quarter-point rate hike, the most hawkish split since Warsh became chairman.
  • St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem told the Financial Times that the selloff signals the need for "earlier, incremental" rate increases.
  • Traders now price a 67% probability of a September rate hike, according to CME FedWatch.

The Market's Verdict

The U.S. Treasury market delivered a stinging rebuke to Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh this week. The 30-year yield surged above 5.20% on Wednesday — its highest level since 2007 — and extended gains through Friday, closing out July with the largest monthly increase since December 2024.

The 10-year yield posted its biggest monthly gain since March. The selloff accelerated not after the Fed's widely expected decision to hold rates steady, but after Warsh's press conference, where he repeatedly declared inflation would be brought down without signaling any readiness to raise rates.

"At this juncture, earlier, incremental, gradual interest-rate action is preferable, less costly and less disruptive than potentially later, larger and abrupt actions."

— Alberto Musalem, President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

Three Dissenters Break Ranks

The Fed voted 9-3 to keep rates unchanged, with three FOMC members dissenting in favor of a quarter-percentage-point hike — the most hawkish split of Warsh's two-month tenure. The dissenters expressed concern on Friday that without an immediate increase in short-term borrowing costs, inflation will remain stuck above the Fed's 2% target, where it has been for more than five years.

Musalem, a non-voting FOMC member, told the Financial Times he had "expressed a preference" for a rate increase at the meeting. His comments — framing the bond selloff as a credibility warning — carry weight because they reflect a growing faction within the Fed that views inaction as riskier than tightening.

Inflation Expectations Shift

What made this week's selloff different from the broader July rout was its composition. Through Tuesday, rising real rates had driven the entire bond decline, while long-term inflation expectations had actually fallen — a sign the market still trusted the Fed to control prices. That changed after Warsh's Wednesday presser.

The 10-year break-even rate — a measure of average expected inflation over the next decade — jumped 0.078 percentage points from Wednesday through Friday. About 60% of the 10-year yield's gain in that period came from rising inflation expectations, according to Barron's analysis. The 30-year break-even rate rose 0.062 percentage points.

Warsh's Credibility Problem

Warsh compounded the market's anxiety by hinting that the Fed may revisit its inflation-targeting framework entirely. He noted that task forces he appointed in May would deliver recommendations by year-end and suggested he might preview ideas at the Fed's Jackson Hole conference in late August.

"That's our number, we're sticking with it," Warsh said of the 2% inflation target, before adding: "Who knows, come after next January, what we might say about strategy."

The combination of tough talk without action and hints about moving the goalposts has rattled bond investors. When the yield curve steepens because of a sharp rise in long-dated yields while short-end rates fall, it typically signals that investors believe the Fed won't act aggressively enough to contain inflation — a perception no central bank chief can afford.

What's Next

Traders are now pricing a 67% probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in September, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech in late August will be closely watched for signals on both the rate path and any framework changes. Mortgage rates have already climbed to 6.58%, up from around 6% at the start of the year, adding pressure on the housing market. The spread between the two-year Treasury yield and the fed funds rate has widened to 70 basis points, the most since November 2022 — a clear signal the bond market wants the Fed to act.
